prime.problem: A neural net does arithmetic on numbers, and Shakespeare is a string. And a model that only ever gets scored on the text it trains on can memorise that text and look like it's improving while learning nothing that carries over.
prime.fits: Second step of the GPT lecture. The previous card loaded 1,115,394 characters and found 65 distinct ones; this card turns them into integer ids (the same stoi/itos idea as the makemore names) and sets aside the text that every later val loss is measured on.
prime.goal: Encode and decode any Shakespeare string by hand from the sorted character list, explain why the last 10% is held out, and write the dozen lines that do both.

attend: Why does sorting the set of characters make the ids reproducible from run to run?
Where exactly does int(0.9*len(data)) cut the file, and why a single slice rather than a shuffle?
Which number would reveal memorisation: the loss on train_data or on val_data, and why?
What do you gain and lose by using 65 characters instead of GPT-2's 50,257 pieces?
What happens when a string contains a character that never appeared in the file?

must: sorted(set(text)) gives a fixed order → a character's position is its id → stoi/itos are exact inverses → decode(encode(s)) == s for any string made of the 65 characters

Training lowers the loss on whatever text it sees → memorising that text also lowers it → train loss alone can't tell learning from memorising → hold out text the model never trains on and watch its loss (val) instead

Small vocabulary (65) → one id per character → long sequences (1,115,394 ids) but a tiny table and no unknown pieces; big sub-word vocabulary (50,257) → about 3.3× fewer ids → longer context per token, at the cost of a much bigger table and a separate tokenizer
The vocabulary is built only from characters seen in the file → it is closed → any new character (é) has no id → encode raises KeyError
elevated: The split is a contiguous slice (data[:n], data[n:]) → val is an unbroken stretch the model never sees, not scattered characters whose neighbours are in train → a more honest measure of generalisation, but its content (61 of the 65 characters) can differ a bit from train
reference: the exact code: stoi = { ch:i for i,ch in enumerate(chars) }, the encode/decode lambdas

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the pipeline from text to train_data and val_data, labelling each arrow with the line of code and each box with its size. Then write two sentences on why the last 10% is held out.
checklist: distinct characters, sorted, give the vocabulary (65)
stoi maps character → id, itos maps back; encode/decode are list lookups
the whole text becomes one tensor of 1,115,394 integer ids
n = int(0.9*len(data)); train is the first 90%, val the unbroken last 10%
val loss exposes overfitting, because memorising train text can't lower it
the trade-off: small vocab means long sequences; sub-word vocab means shorter ones

retrieve.q: Explain why the loss on the training text can't tell you whether the model is overfitting, and what the val loss adds.
answer: memorising the training text lowers the training loss just as learning does
val text is never trained on, so only real generalisation lowers its loss
a train loss that keeps falling while val stalls or rises is the overfitting signal

retrieve.q: Walk encode("hii there") through the code: which dict is used, what does each character become, and how does decode get the string back?
answer: each character is looked up in stoi: h 46, i 47, i 47, space 1, t 58, h 46, e 43, r 56, e 43
the list has 9 ids, one per character
decode looks each id up in itos and ''.joins the characters

retrieve.q: Compare our 65-character tokenizer with GPT-2's 50,257-piece one on the same text. What do you pay for the shorter sequences?
answer: characters: 1,115,394 ids; GPT-2: 338,025 ids, about 3.3× fewer
shorter sequences let a fixed context window cover more text
the cost: a vocabulary 773× larger (a bigger embedding table and output layer) and a trained tokenizer to build and debug

retrieve.q: Where does n = int(0.9*len(data)) land for 1,115,394 characters, and why does int matter?
answer: int truncates to 1,003,854, a valid slice index

compare.q: The makemore split shuffled 32k names into 80/10/10 train/dev/test; this lecture slices one text 90/10 with no shuffle and no test set. What causes the difference, when would you choose each, and how does each fail?
answer: names are independent examples, so shuffling them is safe; Shakespeare is one continuous text, so a slice keeps val's contexts unseen
shuffle-and-split fits collections of separate items; hold out whole documents or a contiguous tail for one long text
a shuffled split of one text would leak neighbouring context into val; a tail split can differ in style or content from train
no test set means repeatedly picking models by val slowly overfits to val too

compare.q: A character tokenizer vs a byte-pair (BPE) tokenizer: what is fundamentally different about how each gets its vocabulary, and how does each fail on unusual input?
answer: characters: the vocabulary is just the distinct characters seen, no training needed
BPE: starts from bytes and learns merges of frequent pairs, so common chunks get one id
characters: an unseen character raises KeyError; byte-level BPE can always fall back to single bytes
characters give long sequences; BPE gives shorter ones but adds its own quirks (the tokenizer lecture's topic)

predict.q: Suppose you build the vocabulary from val_data's text only (the last 10%) and then try to encode the training text. Does it work, and does 'a' keep the id 39?
predict.answer: No on both counts. The val text contains only 61 distinct characters: $, &, 3 and X appear only in the train part. Encoding the train text raises KeyError: '&' at character 75,323 (from 'Senators, &C:'). And since those four characters all sort before a, every lowercase id shifts down by 4: 'a' becomes 35 and 'h' becomes 42. Ids depend on the whole vocabulary, which is why the lecture builds it from the full text before splitting.

apply.task: Use the model to predict ids without running anything: write down encode("Zounds!") from the vocabulary table alone (13 symbols, then A–Z, then a–z). Then run it in your notebook, and also try encode("naïve").
apply.done: You wrote [38, 53, 59, 52, 42, 57, 2] before running it and it matches, and you can say why encode("naïve") raises KeyError: 'ï'.
apply.hint: Uppercase letters start at 13 (A), lowercase at 39 (a). ! is the third character in sorted order, after newline and space.
